module_title: Environmental Law: Constitutional Roots & The Core Acts
introduction: This foundational level explores how environmental protection was woven into the Indian Constitution following the 1972 Stockholm Conference. It introduces the trinity of India's pollution control framework: The Water Act (1974), the Air Act (1981), and the umbrella Environment (Protection) Act (1986).

core_concepts.title: Constitutional Framework (The 42nd Amendment, 1976)
core_concepts.description:
Originally, the Constitution had no direct provision for environmental protection. Inspired by the UN Stockholm Conference (1972), the 42nd Amendment introduced two pillars:
- Article 48A (DPSP): 'The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.'
- Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): It is the duty of every citizen 'to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures.'

core_concepts.title: Article 21: Right to Clean Environment
core_concepts.description: Through judicial activism, the Supreme Court famously expanded the scope of Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty). In *Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991)*, the Court held that the Right to Life includes the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air.

core_concepts.title: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
core_concepts.description:
India's first major environmental law.
- Objective: To prevent and control water pollution and restore the wholesomeness of water.
- Institutional Creation: It created the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs).
- Mechanism: No industry can discharge effluents into water bodies without obtaining 'Consent to Establish' and 'Consent to Operate' from the SPCB.

core_concepts.title: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
core_concepts.description:
Enacted to combat air pollution. Instead of creating new boards, it expanded the powers of the CPCB and SPCBs (created under the Water Act) to also monitor and control air pollution.
- Crucial Amendment: In 1987, the Air Act was amended to officially include **Noise** as an air pollutant.

core_concepts.title: The Environment (Protection) Act (EPA), 1986
core_concepts.description:
Passed in the tragic aftermath of the 1984 **Bhopal Gas Tragedy**.
- Umbrella Legislation: It acts as an overarching framework covering gaps left by the Water and Air Acts. It defines 'Environment' broadly to include water, air, land, and their interrelationship with human beings and other living creatures.
- Delegated Powers: It grants sweeping powers to the Central Government to issue direct orders to close, prohibit, or regulate any industry, and to set emission/effluent standards.

important_entities.name: Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984)
important_entities.significance: The leakage of deadly Methyl Isocyanate (MIC) gas from the Union Carbide plant in Bhopal exposed the severe inadequacy of the Water and Air Acts to handle industrial disasters, forcing Parliament to enact the comprehensive EPA under Article 253 (power to legislate to implement international agreements).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If an exam asks 'Under which Act is Noise Pollution primarily regulated in India?' DO NOT look for a separate 'Noise Pollution Act'. Noise was explicitly added to the definition of 'air pollutant' via the **1987 Amendment to the Air Act, 1981**. Noise pollution rules are issued under the umbrella of the EPA, 1986.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Water flows first (1974), then Air blows (1981), then Bhopal brings the Umbrella (EPA 1986)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this chronological narrative to easily remember the order and rationale behind the three major acts.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which Article was interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the right to a pollution-free environment?', unconditionally select **Article 21**.
